learn.hook: Your milkman calls his milk 'pure', but a chemist would call it a mixture! In science, 'pure' has a very special meaning.
points: A pure substance is made of only one kind of particle and has a fixed composition. Pure substances are elements or compounds.
An element cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical reactions, for example oxygen, copper and mercury.

A compound is formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion by mass. Its properties are different from those of its elements. Water always has hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8.
A mixture has two or more substances that are not chemically combined. Its composition can vary, each component keeps its own properties, and it can be separated by physical methods.
A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout (salt water, air, brass). A heterogeneous mixture has visibly different parts (sand in water, oil in water).

example.q: Think it through: Iron filings and sulphur powder are mixed. Part of the mixture is then heated strongly by the teacher to form iron sulphide. How can a magnet show the difference?
steps: In the unheated mixture, iron keeps its own properties.
So a magnet pulls the iron filings out of the mixture.
On heating, iron and sulphur combine chemically to form a new compound, iron sulphide.
The compound has new properties, and a magnet does not pull iron out of it.
example.answer: The magnet separates iron from the mixture but not from the compound iron sulphide.

learn.reallife: Air, sea water, soil, brass utensils and even the steel of a kitchen spoon are all mixtures.

games.title: Mixtures: true or false?
items: The components of a mixture keep their own properties
That is why a magnet can still pull iron filings out of a mixture of iron and sand.
A compound can be separated into its elements by simple filtering
Elements in a compound are chemically joined and can be separated only by chemical methods.
Air is a homogeneous mixture
The gases in air are evenly mixed, so it has the same composition throughout.
The ratio of elements in a compound can vary from sample to sample
A compound always has its elements in a fixed proportion by mass.
Oil and water form a heterogeneous mixture
They do not mix, and you can see two separate layers.

quiz.q: Which of these is a compound?
quiz.explain: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio. Oxygen is an element; air and brass are mixtures.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any common substance made of two things must be a compound

quiz.q: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?
quiz.explain: Sugar spreads evenly through the water, so every part has the same composition.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any mixture with water is homogeneous

quiz.q: Which property belongs to a compound but NOT to a mixture?
options: Its components keep their own properties
It can be separated by physical methods
Its elements are present in a fixed ratio by mass
quiz.explain: A compound always has a fixed composition. The other three statements describe mixtures.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the properties of compounds and mixtures

quiz.q: Brass is best described as
options: a compound of copper and zinc
a homogeneous mixture (alloy) of copper and zinc
a heterogeneous mixture of copper and sand
quiz.explain: Brass is an alloy. Its metals are evenly mixed but not chemically combined, and its composition can vary.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an alloy is a compound because it looks uniform

quiz.q: Which statement describes an element?
options: It always contains two kinds of atoms
It cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical reactions
quiz.explain: An element is the simplest form of matter; chemical reactions cannot split it into simpler substances.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an element with a compound

quiz.q: The milkman says his milk is 'pure'. For a scientist, milk is
quiz.explain: Milk contains water, fats, proteins, sugar and minerals that are not chemically combined, so it is a mixture.
quiz.mistake: Uses the everyday meaning of 'pure' (unadulterated) instead of the scientific meaning

quiz.q: Why is air called a mixture and not a compound?
options: Its composition can vary and each gas keeps its own properties
quiz.explain: Air has varying amounts of gases such as water vapour, and each gas keeps its own properties, so it is a mixture.
quiz.mistake: Thinks something invisible or gaseous must be a single substance

quiz.q: Hydrogen and oxygen combine in a fixed mass ratio to form water. What is this ratio (hydrogen : oxygen)?
quiz.explain: In water, 1 g of hydrogen always combines with 8 g of oxygen. The 2 : 1 ratio is the number of atoms, not the mass.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the ratio of atoms (2 : 1) with the ratio of masses (1 : 8)

teach.ask: Gappu holds a glass of salt water and a glass of plain water: "Both look the same. Which is pure and which is a mixture? How do I tell?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Salt water is a mixture because salt and water are just mixed and can be separated by evaporating the water. Plain water is a pure compound!
teach.nudge: If I leave the salt water in the sun, what would be left behind? What does that tell me?

learn.hook: Shine a torch through a glass of salt water and you see nothing special. Shine it through diluted milk and a glowing beam appears! What is different?
points: A solution is a homogeneous mixture. The substance that dissolves is the solute; the one it dissolves in is the solvent. In nimbu paani, sugar and salt are solutes and water is the solvent.
Concentration (mass by mass %) = mass of solute ÷ mass of solution × 100. A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture whose particles can be seen, settle down on standing and can be separated by filtration, for example chalk powder in water.
A colloid looks homogeneous but is actually heterogeneous. Its particles are too small to see, do not settle and pass through filter paper, but they scatter light.
The scattering of a beam of light by colloid particles is the Tyndall effect. Milk, fog, smoke, butter, jelly and shaving cream are colloids.

example.q: Think it through: Anu dissolves 20 g of salt in 180 g of water. What is the concentration of the solution in mass by mass percentage?
steps: Mass of solution = solute + solvent = 20 + 180 = 200 g.

learn.reallife: ORS for a child with loose motions is a solution; milk and curd are colloids; and the misty sunbeams seen in hill forests show the Tyndall effect.

quiz.q: Anu dissolves 20 g of salt in 180 g of water. What is the concentration in mass by mass %?
quiz.explain: Concentration = solute ÷ solution × 100 = 20 ÷ (20 + 180) × 100 = 10%.
quiz.mistake: Divides by the mass of the solvent (180 g) instead of the solution (200 g)

quiz.q: Which of these will show the Tyndall effect when a torch beam passes through it?
quiz.explain: Milk is a colloid, and its particles are big enough to scatter light. Particles in true solutions are too small to scatter light.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every liquid scatters light

quiz.q: Chalk powder stirred in water settles at the bottom after some time. This mixture is a
quiz.explain: Suspension particles are large enough to be seen and they settle on standing.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a suspension with a colloid, whose particles do not settle

quiz.q: In a glass of sugar sharbat, which is the solvent?
quiz.explain: The solvent is the substance in which the solute dissolves. Sugar dissolves in water, so water is the solvent.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up solute and solvent

quiz.q: What is a saturated solution?
options: A solution with no solute in it
A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature
quiz.explain: When a solution holds as much solute as it can at a given temperature, it is saturated.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'saturated' just means 'very wet' or 'very dilute'

quiz.q: Fog is a colloid in which
options: tiny water droplets are dispersed in air
quiz.explain: In fog, the dispersed phase is liquid water and the dispersion medium is air (a gas). Such a colloid is an aerosol.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium

quiz.q: Which mixture can be separated by filtration?
quiz.explain: Chalk particles in a suspension are big enough to be trapped by filter paper. Solution and colloid particles pass through.
quiz.mistake: Thinks filter paper can remove dissolved substances

quiz.q: Sunbeams entering a misty forest look like bright streaks. Why?
options: The forest floor reflects all light upwards
Mist droplets scatter the light (Tyndall effect)
quiz.explain: Mist is a colloid. Its tiny droplets scatter sunlight, making the path of the light visible.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the visible beam with scattering by colloid particles

teach.ask: Gappu looks at three glasses: salt water, muddy water and milk: "They are all mixtures. How are they different from each other?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Salt water is a solution, muddy water is a suspension that settles, and milk is a colloid that scatters a torch beam. The Tyndall test is so cool!
teach.nudge: If I shine a torch through each glass, what would I see differently?

learn.hook: How does a dairy take the cream out of milk, and how do salt makers on the Gujarat coast get salt from the sea? Each mixture needs its own clever trick!
points: Evaporation removes a liquid and leaves the dissolved solid behind, as in getting salt from sea water. Crystallisation gives purer crystals than evaporating to dryness, because impurities stay in the remaining liquid.
Centrifugation spins a mixture very fast so heavier particles collect at the bottom. It separates cream from milk and is used in blood tests.

A separating funnel separates two liquids that do not mix, such as kerosene and water. Sublimation separates a substance that changes directly from solid to vapour, such as camphor, naphthalene or ammonium chloride, from one that does not.
Chromatography separates coloured parts of a mixture, such as dyes in ink, because they travel at different speeds up the paper.

Distillation separates two liquids that mix but have well-separated boiling points (acetone and water). Fractional distillation is used when boiling points are close, as in separating the gases of air or the parts of petroleum.

example.q: Think it through: How would you separate a mixture of sand, common salt and camphor?
steps: Camphor sublimes, so an adult heats the mixture gently under a funnel; camphor vapour collects on the cool funnel.
Add water to the remaining sand and salt and stir. Salt dissolves, sand does not.
Filter: sand stays on the filter paper.
Evaporate the filtrate (with adult help) to get the salt back.
example.answer: Sublimation for camphor, then dissolving and filtration for sand, then evaporation for salt.

learn.reallife: Water treatment plants use sedimentation, loading with alum and filtration, and refineries use fractional distillation to get petrol, diesel and kerosene from crude oil.

games.prompt: Arrange the steps (done with adult supervision) from first to last
items: Dissolve the impure salt in water
Filter out the insoluble dirt
Heat the filtrate gently until it is concentrated
Let it cool slowly so crystals form
Filter out the crystals and dry them

quiz.q: Which method separates cream from milk?
quiz.explain: Spinning the milk very fast separates the lighter cream from the rest of the milk.
quiz.mistake: Thinks filter paper can remove cream, a colloid

quiz.q: How would you separate a mixture of kerosene and water?
quiz.explain: Kerosene and water do not mix and form two layers. A separating funnel lets the lower water layer drain out first.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that the liquids are immiscible and form layers

quiz.q: Which method separates camphor from common salt?
quiz.explain: Camphor turns directly into vapour on gentle heating and can be collected on a cool surface; salt does not sublime.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that camphor sublimes

quiz.q: Which technique shows that black ink is a mixture of different dyes?
quiz.explain: In paper chromatography, each dye travels a different distance up the paper, so the colours separate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks black ink is a single colour, a pure substance

quiz.q: Salt makers along the coast of Gujarat obtain salt from sea water mainly by
quiz.explain: Sea water is let into shallow pans, the Sun evaporates the water, and salt is left behind.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dissolved salt can be filtered out

quiz.q: Which method is used to separate the different gases from air?
quiz.explain: Air is cooled to become a liquid, then warmed slowly; gases like nitrogen, argon and oxygen boil off at different temperatures.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that gases can be liquefied and separated by boiling points

quiz.q: Why is crystallisation better than evaporating to dryness for getting pure copper sulphate?
options: Soluble impurities stay in the liquid, and the solid is not overheated
It makes the crystals bigger than the beaker
quiz.explain: In crystallisation, pure crystals form while impurities remain dissolved. Evaporating to dryness leaves impurities mixed in and can damage some solids.
quiz.mistake: Thinks evaporation and crystallisation give equally pure products

quiz.q: Acetone (boiling point 56 °C) and water (100 °C) mix completely. Which method separates them?
quiz.explain: They mix, so a funnel will not work. Their boiling points are far apart, so distillation boils off the acetone first.
quiz.mistake: Picks a separating funnel for liquids that actually mix

teach.ask: Gappu spilled sand into the salt jar: "Oh no! Can you help me get the salt back without eating sand?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Dissolve the salt in water, filter out the sand, then evaporate the water to get the salt back. My salt jar is saved!
teach.nudge: After the sand is filtered out, the salt is still dissolved in the water. How do I get it back?
